title: The detachable toe peg
problem: Aven has one shallow drawer and a wide tool shelf. The narrow drawer will take the flat practice sole, but some handlers need to see where the small peg belongs.
action: Use the catalogue’s 29 cm and 10 cm spans to turn the plain sole template inside a fictional 31 by 12 cm opening. The peg travels separately.

labels: Turn the sole across the rail

bets: Pack the sole longways and tie the peg to a side tab
Send a wide board that keeps the peg beside its hole
results: The sole slides through the gap. A tab on the drawer points to the matching loose peg when Aven pulls it out.
The peg and hole stay side by side. Aven can point to how the two parts meet, using an extra shelf slot.

object.title: Sandal (mtalawanda / mtawanda) or Clog (kiatu cha mti)
object.observation: A record for one sandal names wood and glass beads. The museum describes the foot support as a wooden base with a separate antelope-shaped toe peg.
object.limit: The image does not establish who wore this sandal. The museum treats the interpretation of preserved sole designs as an inference.
object.altText: Brown wooden sandal with a raised animal-shaped toe support and small beads.

title: The reversible rest
problem: The drawer keeper wants the support edge kept in view. A hanger on the shared shelf can show the whole outline but takes another slot.
action: The museum lists overall size with no named axes. Turn a plain outline made from the 13.1 and 16.3 cm spans. It only tests an outline.

labels: Long listed span along the rail
Long listed span across the rail

bets: Fit the short listed span across the drawer and leave an edge tab
Use the separate wide shelf with all three catalogue spans
results: The drawer clears, and the tab points out a support edge. The other listed span stays on the ticket.
All three spans are legible from the shelf. The keeper leaves the axes unassigned.

object.title: Headrest
object.observation: The catalogue lists wood and colorant and gives three overall dimensions for this particular headrest.
object.limit: The record attributes a style. It does not name the maker or document how this individual object was used.
object.altText: Wooden headrest with a curved top over a carved upright and a double-lobed base.

title: The hat profile
problem: Aven must keep a high rim visible without squeezing it through the opening. Two plain profiles can show different parts of the catalogue dimensions.
action: Cut a side outline to the catalogue’s 17.1 cm top diameter and 9.6 cm height. Turn it against the opening on the practice drawer.
bets: Slide in a side profile with a top-diameter tab
Send an open display of the top circle and side height
results: The side profile clears. The next keeper lifts the tab to see which dimension came from the top.
The round top and height sit on two adjacent sheets. Both can be checked before the board goes away.

object.title: Hat
object.dateKind: Recorded latest date by which the hat existed
object.dimensions: Overall: 9.6 cm (3 3/4 in.); Diameter of top: 17.1 cm (6 3/4 in.)
object.observation: The museum records this woven hat as made by 1928. Its catalogue associates its preserved condition with work made for visitors passing through Ekibondo.
object.limit: The recorded latest date and association with an export setting do not name this maker or make the hat representative of all Mangbetu work.
object.altText: Woven rounded hat with differently coloured bands across the surface.

title: The bracelet outline
problem: A drawer slot is ready. Aven wants its paper aperture to leave a gap near a fragile fibre edge.
action: Turn the practice outline from the recorded 10.5 cm width and 7 cm height. The fixture checks the outline and does not contact the bracelet.
bets: Use the narrow drawer and keep the fibre edge marked
Send the enlarged outline and material slip to the wide shelf
results: The marked edge clears the opening. A handler can see the fibre warning before drawing the pattern out.
A handler can point to the brass and fibre on the enlarged pattern. One extra shelf space is used.

object.title: Bracelet
object.observation: The Met lists brass and fibre for this bracelet, whose maximum documented width is 10.5 cm.
object.limit: The gallery discusses several sites and kinds of Sao work. The record does not establish a particular ritual use or wearer for this bracelet.
object.altText: Curving bracelet with a dark green and brown surface.

title: The collar strip
problem: Aven is lending a plain length strip. One drawer has space for it, while a wide shelf can show the strip next to the separate note about uncertain attribution.
action: Set the paper strip to the catalogue length, 45.7 cm. Its 5 cm width belongs to this workshop strip.
bets: Place the length strip in the drawer with its ticket
Keep the strip and two possible attributions together on the shelf
results: The full-length strip lies flat. The ticket still identifies Xhosa or Mfengu authorship.
Both possible attributions stay beside the strip. Aven reserves the space for readers comparing the catalogue words.

object.title: Collar (Ingqosha)
object.observation: The catalogue gives a length of 45.7 cm and lists sinew, glass beads and a button. The artist field reads Xhosa or Mfengu artist.
object.limit: The museum does not choose between Xhosa and Mfengu authorship or name a wearer.
object.altText: Beaded collar with patterned rows and a button fastener.

title: The hollow-looking tally
problem: Veya is lending a cutaway model. A quick tally can say how many copies left. A component slip can tell the return keeper to look for the insert as well.
action: Slide the workshop tally between whole copies and the loose pieces in the demonstration model. This ledger has no price column.

labels: Count the copies and core inserts

bets: Send three assembled-copy marks to the gate desk
Send both rows to the return shelf
results: Veya can sign out three model copies quickly. She leaves the insert count for the full record.
The return keeper checks each insert against one of the three model shells before hanging the set.

object.title: Currency
object.dateKind: Qualified catalogue dating of this currency
object.observation: The museum catalogues this individual currency object as brass around a fired terracotta core, probably from the nineteenth century.
object.limit: The material record supplies composition. It does not supply the object’s original value, its exchange rate or a transaction.
object.altText: A brass band arches over rounded supports. Several ridges run along the band.

title: Five ingots on one line
problem: Veya needs the practice set to travel intact. One keeper counts five objects. Another needs to check the two paper sleeves separately.
action: Count the four pieces in this museum view, then move the model tally between all five catalogued pieces and the two sleeves. The dimensions in the collection record are averages.

labels: Count the group in one line

bets: Post the five-block group count at the gate desk
Post the two-sleeve count at the return shelf
results: The gate desk records a five-block set. Veya clips on a note that the photograph shows four. The gallery’s dimensions are averages across the catalogued group.
The return keeper counts two in the first sleeve and three in the second. A missing block can be traced to its sleeve.

object.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art
object.title: Ingots
object.dimensions: H x W x D: 3.2 x 2.5 x 0.6 cm (1 1/4 x 1 x 1/4 in.) (average dimensions)
object.place: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Luba attribution
object.observation: The Smithsonian describes a group of five copper-alloy ingots with casting ridges visible underneath. The measurements shown are group averages.
object.limit: The average dimensions do not describe every item. The record does not state an exchange value for this group.
object.altText: Four X-shaped ingots appear in this photograph. The museum catalogue lists five for the accession.

title: Both sides of one thaler
problem: The gate desk wants one count of the practice token. The return shelf needs the portrait and eagle to remain visible when a neighbour comes to check the markings.
action: Match the portrait in the museum view. Flip the practice token to the eagle described in the record. One tally counts objects and another counts these two labelled views.

labels: Count the portrait and eagle views

bets: Send a single-token receipt with the type reference
Hang two labelled views on the return shelf
results: A runner checks out one object. The note preserves 1780 as the type reference beside the catalogue link.
The return keeper can find both faces and still groups them under one accession. No extra token is counted.

object.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art
object.title: Coin
object.dateKind: Catalogue date and coin type inscription
object.attribution: Habsburg thaler type showing Maria Theresa, individual mint or engraver not identified by this record
object.place: Austria and Ethiopia appear in the Smithsonian geography fields
object.observation: The catalogue identifies a silver thaler with Maria Theresa on one face and a double-headed eagle on the other. It explains the importance of this coin type in Ethiopian silver circulation.
object.limit: Treat 1780 as the catalogue date and type inscription. This source does not document a specific Ethiopian transaction or a confidently identified minting date for this individual piece.
object.altText: One face of a round silver coin. It shows the portrait of Maria Theresa.

title: The pan already weighs something
problem: The gate desk must read a full pan quickly. The return keeper needs to know how many of the practice marks belong to the pan itself.
action: Slide the beam figures between the whole practice load and the reading with its empty pan counted separately.
bets: Keep the gross and empty-pan marks together at the gate
Post the net load with the measured empty-pan row
results: The gate desk can compare gross loads with the same pan. Veya keeps the empty-pan figure visible on the receipt.
The return keeper reads six marks of contents and can reconstruct the nine-mark gross reading from both rows.

object.title: Scale for Gold Measurement
object.observation: The Met catalogues this Akan scale for gold measurement in brass, string and pigment. The dimensions field lists 12.4 cm high and 5.7 cm in diameter.
object.limit: The record does not give a load for these pans, a scale calibration, or an individual transaction.
object.altText: Small hanging scale with round brass pans and suspension strings.

title: The lid gets its own line
problem: A labelled box form and lid form can ride as one packet. When somebody takes them apart for a display, the return account needs both pieces.
action: Move the strip between packet and part tallies for two practice sets. The Met describes this particular accession as an Asante-Akan gold-dust box.
bets: Tag the two closed packets at the gate desk
Leave a body-and-lid count where the sets come back
results: The runner sees two packets. Each packet keeps the two-part reference on a folded slip.
The return keeper checks two lids before sending the bodies back into storage. No stray lid is counted as a new box.

object.title: Abamphruwa (gold-dust box)
object.observation: This brass abamphruwa is catalogued as an Asante-Akan gold-dust box. Its accession covers two parts, a and b.
object.limit: The catalogue does not establish a particular owner, load or transaction for this box.
object.altText: Small rectangular brass box with a raised lid on top.

title: A braid’s trace in clay
problem: Coru wants one projection showing where a loose strand impressed the model’s surface. A second board preserves the clay edge that reveals what has the texture.
action: Move the plain practice strip until either the braid repeat or the clay edge lines up. Each register preserves a different detail.
bets: Face the repeat towards the front seat
Keep the clay edge and surface trace together at the bench
results: The front seat can follow the repeat. The tab marks it as an impression in clay.
A visitor can point to the edge and see that the pattern belongs to clay, even where the braid left a clear trace.

object.title: Globular vessel with twine impressions
object.attribution: Middle Niger artist(s), qualified attribution in the culture field
object.observation: The terracotta vessel preserves impressed patterns that resemble woven basketry. The Met describes braided fibre used to stamp such designs into the surface.
object.limit: The impressed texture is a mark on terracotta. It does not establish what this vessel held or require a claim that the form itself was a basket.
object.altText: Round terracotta vessel with overlapping impressed patterns.

title: The join between groove and platform
problem: Coru has a small projection of two documented details. From one seat the grooves show plainly. From the bench, the smooth platform and its supports read together.
action: Bring the practice overlay into register with the grooves first, then with the smooth platform. Keep the catalogue’s attribution separate from the visible marks.
bets: Face the grooves towards the seat with the attribution slip
Place the platform and supports together at the handling bench
results: The grooves are easy to find. The slip says the museum attributes the work through comparison.
The bench visitor can point out the four supports, then check the separate attribution slip before retelling it.

object.title: Zoomorphic headrest
object.attribution: Attributed to “Unobadula” in The Met’s artist field, the public account discusses a stylistically related group of sculptors
object.place: South Africa, Nguni peoples, mid-nineteenth-century makers near present-day Durban
object.observation: The wood headrest has a smooth platform above four legs and incised grooves around the sides. The Met explains the attribution through stylistic comparison.
object.limit: The catalogue’s comparison does not turn a stylistic attribution into an individual autograph or show that this was the headrest in a related historical illustration.
object.altText: Carved wooden headrest with four curved supports, a smooth top and groups of incised lines.

title: A figure changes at an angle
problem: Coru has two plain silhouettes for visitors. A front seat can read the face first. Readers at the handling bench can compare both poses with the museum credit.
action: Move the paper overlay from the frontal figure line to the profile line. The practice marks are simple shapes and preserve the two orientations.

labels: Line up the figure in profile

bets: Place the frontal outline on the seat board
Place both outlines and the attribution on the handling bench
results: The first visitor finds the frontal pose. An arrow points away from the nearest figure to the profile outline.
The reader can compare frontal and profile orientations. A separate line links to the catalogue name, Master of the Heraldic Ship.

object.title: Saltcellar with Portuguese Figures
object.observation: The Met describes this Benin saltcellar as the work of an ivory carver its catalogue calls “Master of the Heraldic Ship.” The two higher-status Portuguese figures face outward and their two attendants appear in profile.
object.limit: The catalogue describes a possible set for a patron. It does not identify the patron, or establish that the labels name a historically documented maker.
object.altText: Historical ivory saltcellar carved with figures around the exterior.

title: The strand behind the bead
problem: Coru’s little mark board can show the cord from a distance or make room for three material tabs on a bench where visitors can check them.
action: Line up a plain loop of cord and a material mark. The museum names wood, ceramic and raffia. The practice strip has no proposed wearer or exchange trail.
bets: Mount the loop line and keep the material tab nearby
Keep the wood, ceramic and raffia tabs beside the trace
results: The loop shape reads from the first seat. The material tab keeps the source at hand for a follow-up.
A reader can separate the three material labels before following the continuous line. The sign leaves the wearer and origin open.

object.title: Necklace
object.place: Angola or Democratic Republic of the Congo
object.observation: The museum attributes the necklace to a Chokwe artist and lists wood, ceramic and raffia. It gives Angola or the Democratic Republic of the Congo as the geography.
object.limit: The catalogue does not identify the maker or wearer by name or establish this necklace’s journey.
object.altText: Strung necklace made of different shaped components on a loop.

title: A soundbox below an arc
problem: Coru wants a plain guide to a two-part form. A spectator sees the long curve first. A closer reader can trace the place where lines meet the soundbox.
action: Move a practice strip between the arc and the diagonal-string line. A second printed shape marks the soundbox in each view.

labels: Register the line to the soundbox

bets: Face the neck curve towards the first seat
Mount the soundbox and diagonal trace beside each other
results: The arc is visible from the seat. A second pointer brings the eye back to the soundbox.
The bench reader can follow a diagonal line from neck to soundbox. The guide leaves the pitch of this instrument unclaimed.

object.title: Ennanga
object.medium: Wood, vegetal fiber, snake skin, hide
object.dimensions: Height: 29 15/16 in. (76 cm) Width: 8 1/4 in. (21 cm)
object.observation: The Met describes this Ganda ennanga as having a soundbox and a curved neck, with diagonal strings. A small ring under each tuning peg contributes a buzz in the described instrument form.
object.limit: The record is not an acoustic measurement or a recording of a performance on this individual harp.
object.altText: Arched harp with a curved neck above the soundbox and diagonal strings.

title: The second surface
problem: Sivra has two places to put a cue card. An opener at the rail wants the first impact. A reader at the bench wants the short tail too.
action: Move the practice shutter over the strike marker and the later tail of two superposed model layers. The museum’s two hides prompted the fixture.
bets: Send the strike trace to the first cue rail
Send the tail and strike together to the listening drawer
results: Sivra follows the first mark in the practice score. The role of the second layer stays on the accompanying slip.
A listener traces through the tail and sees the two model layers. The label gives Kampala as a purchase place.

object.title: Drum (ngoma)
object.dateKind: Recorded latest date from purchase documentation
object.dimensions: Diameter: 31.2 cm (12 5/16 in.); Overall: 40 cm (15 3/4 in.)
object.attribution: Unidentified maker, museum records purchase in Kampala
object.place: Purchased in Kampala, Uganda. Precise place of making unrecorded.
object.observation: The museum describes two hides over a hollow wooden body, with the outer layer secured by plant fiber. It records purchase in Kampala and distinguishes this example from sacred royal drums.
object.limit: A purchase location is a custody clue. It does not determine who made the drum or where it was made.
object.altText: A drum with a rounded top, textured sides and a slender loose strap.

title: One joined ring, two contacts
problem: A small cue card can show the joined projections making one stimulus. A full drawer card can also show what two separated contacts look like in the empty rig.
action: Check an early joined pair and a longer two-contact trace from plain test tabs. They demonstrate alternative contacts, not this ring’s former sound.
bets: Use the joined pulse at the cue rail
Keep both possible contacts at the listening drawer
results: The cue rail has one compact sign. Elsewhere on the receipt, the two historical comparisons stay labelled as analogies.
The listener sees one tight pair and separated marks. Sivra keeps the two proposed comparisons distinct from measured sound.

object.institution: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art
object.title: Ring
object.attribution: Inland Niger Delta style, maker unrecorded
object.observation: The Smithsonian records a copper-alloy ring with incised lines and joined projections. It notes analogies to both paired finger percussion and horse bells.
object.limit: The suggested uses are comparisons with related objects. Surface patina alone cannot determine this object’s exact use or archaeological context.
object.altText: Copper-alloy ring with joined projections and incised lines.

title: A string line and a body line
problem: Sivra wants two readable signs for a visiting reader. The first catches an onset. A second sign lets a reader follow the body tail and find the instrument record.
action: Move the shutter over an invented pair of traces. A quick line marks the pluck and a wider line shows when the demonstration body continues.
bets: Hang the onset trace at the cue rail
Keep the onset and longer tail at the listening drawer
results: The cue reader finds the start. Sivra leaves a link beside the onset for the museum’s description of the gourd and hide.
A visitor finds the gourd-body note after tracing the later marks. The guide labels the practice pulse as its own invention.

object.title: Kora
object.observation: The Met identifies this nineteenth-century Mandinka kora from Senegambia and describes a gourd resonator covered with hide, a neck, handles and a bridge.
object.limit: The catalogue shows the construction of this instrument and discusses the kora broadly. The fictional trace is not evidence of its historical tuning or performance.
object.altText: Tall string instrument above a gourd resonator, with a neck and handles.

title: Across the trough
problem: Sivra can put a narrow launch cue at the rail or keep the launch and the second leg on a wider bench sheet.
action: Move the shutter over a plain bridge-marker signal, then follow the longer marker attributed to a fictional trough. The hourglass form comes from the hoddu’s individual record.
bets: Give the cue reader the bridge-marker trace
Keep both lengths of trace in the drawer
results: The rail card shows a clear short start. A side tab directs the reader to the museum’s hourglass-body description.
A visitor follows both windows and finds the official account of the narrow trough. The country line stays qualified.

object.title: Hoddu (Xalam)
object.place: Mali, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau or the Senegambia
object.observation: The Met identifies a Fulbe hoddu with a narrow hourglass-shaped trough carved from wood and an animal-hide soundboard. Its geography field lists Mali, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau or Senegambia.
object.limit: The catalogue does not fix one country in this geography field or preserve what this individual instrument sounded like on a given day.
object.altText: Wooden lute with a narrow hourglass-shaped body and a long neck.

title: Separate sticks on the same pulse line
problem: Sivra needs a clean cue for one practice line or a sheet showing how staggered starts can still belong to one grouped set.
action: Look for a start on one fictional strip and a set of later starts on the other. Each strip stands for a plain loose test part, not a copy of the instrument.
bets: Place one legible start at the rail
Keep grouped separate starts on a drawer sheet
results: A cue reader finds the first start without following every model mark. A tab credits the museum’s separate-stick description.
The listener can distinguish multiple starts and see that the record groups them as one instrument, each string with its own stick.

object.title: Ubo akwara (pluriarc)
object.observation: The Met catalogues this late nineteenth-century object as an Igbo ubo akwara from Nigeria. Its description notes that each string in the pluriarc has its own flexible stick.
object.limit: The record does not give the pitches or the account of a named player. The trace compares original fictional timing markers only.
object.altText: Pluriarc with several curved sticks rising separately from the wooden body.
